definition: Dissipate means to scatter and drift apart until it is gone, the way fog, smoke, or a strong feeling gradually thins into nothing; it can also mean to waste money or resources through careless living.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word dissipate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know dissipate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: By mid-morning, the thick fog over the harbor had begun to dissipate, and the fishing boats slowly came into view.
Fade simply means to grow fainter, but dissipate goes further, suggesting something thins out until it is entirely gone.
Vanish is stronger and more sudden than dissipate, which describes a slow, gradual disappearance rather than an instant one.

To evaporate is literally to turn from liquid into vapor, and figuratively to disappear as if into thin air - savings or confidence can evaporate. Dissipate keeps the scattering visible: fog, smoke, or tension thins and drifts apart until nothing is left. Evaporation is the vanishing trick; dissipation is the slow drift apart.

To dwindle is to shrink steadily in size or number - a crowd dwindles, supplies dwindle - and what dwindles is still there, only smaller. To dissipate is to thin out and scatter until it is entirely gone. A dwindling fog has shrunk; a dissipated fog is gone from the sky altogether.

To squander is to waste money, time, or chances through carelessness, and it is always about resources. Dissipate shares that second sense - the heir dissipated his fortune - but adds the image of scattering it to nothing. And unlike squander, dissipate's main job is describing fog, smoke, and feelings thinning away.

Dissipate means to scatter and drift apart until it is gone, the way fog, smoke, or a strong feeling gradually thins into nothing; it can also mean to waste money or resources through careless living.
Dissipate also has a second, older sense: to waste money or resources through careless overindulgence.
The young heir dissipated his entire inheritance in barely three years, pouring it into gambling trips and lavish parties.
By the time he turned thirty, a fortune built over generations had been thrown away completely.

This example shows the word's separate 'waste or squander' sense, which is different from the fading-fog sense: here nothing fades on its own; instead, a person carelessly scatters wealth until nothing is left.
Neutral; academic and literary
Unlike dispel, which implies someone actively banishes a feeling or myth on purpose, dissipate suggests something fades away gradually on its own, like fog burning off in the sun.
It is also distinct from disperse, which describes a crowd or group physically scattering in different directions.
Watch for the second sense too: to dissipate a fortune is to waste it through careless living.

Ana Reyes had dreaded the regional spelling final for weeks, and when she walked onstage her stage fright arrived right on schedule.
Her hands buzzed, the lights felt hot, and the first word sounded like it came from underwater.
Then, somewhere in the second round, the fear began to dissipate.
It did not break or vanish in one merciful instant; it thinned out syllable by syllable, loosening its grip a little with each word she landed.
By the final round she looked up, realized she was enjoying herself, and could not point to any moment when the dread had actually left the building.
